intro: Eight exam-style problems bring together the lesson's mechanical energy and momentum. Solve them as in the exam: justify which conservation law you choose and why it holds in the situation, solve for the unknown quantity before substituting the numbers, and assess whether the result is reasonable. Open the model answer and the marking scheme only when your solution is ready.

tasks.title: A zip line across a lake
tasks.source_note: The zip line and its numbers are an invented example.
tasks.text:
A summer activity at a ski resort is a zip line, on which a rider fastened in a harness glides across a lake hanging from a trolley that runs on wheels. The start is $36.0\,\text{m}$ higher than the end of the line, and the cable is $410\,\text{m}$ long. The rider starts from rest. At the end a spring brake stops the trolley.

- mass of the rider, the harness and the trolley together $82.0\,\text{kg}$
- speed just before the brake (the trolley's GPS meter) $15.0\,\text{m/s}$
- braking lasts $1.6\,\text{s}$, and the cable is horizontal at the end

parts.text: What would the rider's speed be at the end if there were no air resistance and no resistance from the trolley's wheels?
hints: Which forms of energy does the rider have at the start and at the end when there are no resistive forces? Which one turns into the other?
Mechanical energy is conserved: $mgh = \tfrac12 mv^2$.
The mass cancels from the equation, so solve for $v$ in symbols first. Use the height difference $h$, not the length of the cable.

criteria.detail: Mechanical energy is conserved: $mgh = \tfrac12 mv^2$, so $v = \sqrt{2gh}$.
$v = \sqrt{2 \cdot 9.81\,\tfrac{\text{m}}{\text{s}^2} \cdot 36.0\,\text{m}}$
$v \approx 26.6\,\text{m/s}$ to three significant figures

parts.text: How much work do air resistance and the wheel resistance do during the ride? What is the average magnitude of the resistive forces along the cable?
hints: What happens to the mechanical energy when the resistive forces do work? Is this work positive or negative?

Work–energy principle: the work done by the resistive forces is the change in mechanical energy, $W_\text{other} = E_\text{final} - E_\text{initial}$. The average force follows from the work and the distance: $F = |W_\text{other}| : s$.
At the start the rider is at rest, and at the end the zero level of potential energy is at the end of the line, so each state has only one form of energy. The distance $s$ is the length of the cable.

criteria.text: Justifies with the work–energy principle: the work done by the resistive forces is negative and equal to the change in mechanical energy.

criteria.detail: $W_\text{other} = \tfrac12 mv^2 - mgh$ and $F = |W_\text{other}| : s$
$\tfrac12 mv^2 = 9225\,\text{J}$, $mgh \approx 28\,960\,\text{J}$, so $W_\text{other} \approx -19.7\,\text{kJ}$ and $F \approx 48.1\,\text{N}$
The work in kilojoules and the force in newtons to three significant figures; the sign of the work negative

parts.text: What is the average horizontal force of the brake on the trolley, when the trolley also stops the rider and the harness? Compare the force with the combined weight of the rider, the harness and the trolley.
hints: Which quantity changes when the brake stops the trolley and the rider, and how long does it take?
Impulse–momentum principle: the impulse of the average force is the change in momentum, $F_\text{avg}\,\Delta t = |\Delta p|$.
When stopping, the final momentum is zero, so $|\Delta p| = mv$. Use the speed from the GPS meter. For the comparison, also calculate the weight $mg$.

criteria.detail: Impulse–momentum principle: $F_\text{avg}\,\Delta t = |\Delta p| = mv$
$F_\text{avg} \approx 770\,\text{N}$ to two significant figures like the time $1.6\,\text{s}$
The force is almost as large as the weight $mg \approx 804\,\text{N}$, which feels like a clear but safe jolt.

parts.text: The zip-line attendant says: “Light riders arrive more slowly, because gravity pulls them less strongly.” Assess the claim.
hints: What happens to the mass in the energy equation when there are no resistive forces? What would the claim say about this situation?
Does air resistance depend on the rider's mass in the same way as gravity does? Think about how the work of the resistive forces compares with the rider's mechanical energy.
Compare a light and a heavy rider: for which one is the same work done by resistance a larger part of the mechanical energy? Decide whether the observation or its explanation holds.

criteria.text: Justifies that without resistive forces the mass cancels out of the energy equation, so the final speed $\sqrt{2gh}$ does not depend on the mass.
Justifies that the work done by the resistive forces reduces the mechanical energy of a lighter rider relatively more, because air resistance is not proportional to the mass.

criteria.detail: The observation may be true, but the reasoning is wrong: the cause is air resistance, not weaker gravity.

tasks.title: A curling throw
tasks.source_note: The numbers of the throw are an invented example. The mass of a curling stone and the order of magnitude of the coefficient of friction match the real sport.
tasks.text:
In curling a granite stone is slid along the ice. A player releases the stone at $2.40\,\text{m/s}$. The stone slides straight for $27.0\,\text{m}$ and hits an opponent's stone at rest head-on. Just before the impact its speed is $0.62\,\text{m/s}$. A video shows that just after the collision the thrown stone continues in the same direction at $0.05\,\text{m/s}$.

- mass of each stone $19.0\,\text{kg}$
- the stones are not swept, and the ice is the same along the whole distance

parts.text: What is the coefficient of friction between the stone and the ice?
hints: Which force does work as the stone slides on the ice, and what does its work do to the kinetic energy of the stone?

Work–energy principle: the initial kinetic energy minus the work of friction is the kinetic energy at the moment of impact, $\tfrac12 mv_0^2 - \mu mg s = \tfrac12 mv_1^2$. The friction force is $\mu N$, and on horizontal ice the normal force equals the weight.
The mass cancels from the equation: solve for $\mu$ in symbols first. Use the initial speed, the speed at impact and the distance $27.0\,\text{m}$.

criteria.detail: Work–energy principle: $\tfrac12 mv_0^2 - \mu mg s = \tfrac12 mv_1^2$, so $\mu = \dfrac{v_0^2 - v_1^2}{2gs}$

criteria.text: Justifies that the friction force $\mu mg$ is constant and does the negative work $-\mu mgs$, because the normal force equals the weight.

criteria.detail: $\mu \approx 0.010$, two significant figures like the speed $0.62\,\text{m/s}$; the coefficient of friction has no unit

parts.text: What is the speed of the struck stone just after the collision? Is the collision elastic?
hints: Which forces act on the stones during the collision, and how long does the collision last compared with the sliding of the stone?

When the impulse of friction is small, the total momentum of the stones is conserved: before the collision only the thrown stone moves, afterwards both do. Write $p_\text{before} = p_\text{after}$ using the mass $m$ of each stone.

The masses are equal and cancel, so solve for the speed of the struck stone in symbols. To judge elasticity, think about which quantity is conserved in an elastic collision, and compare it before and after.

criteria.text: Justifies conservation of momentum: the impulse of friction is negligible during the short collision.
Compares the kinetic energies: after $\approx 3.11\,\text{J}$, before $\approx 3.65\,\text{J}$, so about $85\,\%$ is conserved, and the collision is nearly but not perfectly elastic.

parts.text: How far does the struck stone slide before it stops?
hints: What stops the struck stone, and what does its kinetic energy turn into?
Work–energy principle: the kinetic energy is used up in the work of friction, $\tfrac12 mv_2'^2 = \mu mg s$.
The ice is the same along the whole distance, so use the coefficient of friction from part a) and the speed from part b). Solve for $s$ in symbols; the mass cancels.

criteria.detail: $\tfrac12 m v_2'^2 = \mu mg s$, so $s = \dfrac{v_2'^2}{2\mu g}$
$s \approx 1.6\,\text{m}$ to two significant figures

parts.text: Players often sweep the ice in front of a sliding stone, which reduces the coefficient of friction. Explain with energy why the stone then slides further, even though the brooms do not touch the stone.
hints: Into what does the kinetic energy of the stone turn as it slides, and which force causes this?
The work of friction is $-\mu mg s$. What changes in this expression when the ice is swept, and what stays the same?

The kinetic energy of the stone at the start is the same in both cases. How does the distance $s$ at which all the kinetic energy has been used up depend on the coefficient of friction? Do the brooms add energy to the stone?

criteria.text: Explains that the kinetic energy of the stone is transformed into internal energy through the negative work $-\mu mg s$ done by friction, and a smaller $\mu$ means less work per metre.

criteria.detail: The same kinetic energy lasts for a longer distance; sweeping does not add energy to the stone but reduces the work done by friction per metre.

tasks.title: A braking test on wet asphalt
tasks.source_note: The data are an invented example: the numbers were calculated from a model in which the reaction time and the deceleration are constant, and variation like that of real measurements was added to them.
tasks.text:
On the skid track of a driving school the stopping distance on wet asphalt was studied. The same driver drove the same car along a straight, horizontal track at a constant speed $v_0$. A light came on, and the driver braked as hard as possible. The distance from the light coming on to the car stopping was measured with a measuring wheel to the nearest $0.5\,\text{m}$.

| $v_0\ (\text{km/h})$ | $s_\text{p}\ (\text{m})$ |
|---|---|
| $30$ | $12.5$ |
| $40$ | $20.0$ |
| $50$ | $27.5$ |
| $60$ | $36.5$ |
| $70$ | $46.5$ |
| $80$ | $58.5$ |
| $90$ | $72.0$ |

parts.text: Present the stopping distance as a function of the initial speed in a graph. Justify why a straight line does not fit the points.
hints: Calculate the differences between the distances of successive measurements. Are they equal when the speed always increases by $10\,\text{km/h}$?
The stopping distance is the reaction distance plus the braking distance. How does each depend on the initial speed?
Join the first and the last point with a straight line. Are the other points on the same side of it, or on both sides?

criteria.detail: $v_0$ with its unit on the horizontal axis, $s_\text{p}\ (\text{m})$ on the vertical axis.

criteria.text: Justifies with the curvature of the graph and with physics: the braking distance grows with the square of the speed, so the stopping distance grows faster than the speed.

parts.text: From the data, form a quantity whose graph against the initial speed is a straight line when the driver's reaction time and the car's deceleration stay the same. Present it in a graph and fit a straight line to the points.
hints: The reaction distance is proportional to the speed and the braking distance to the square of the speed. What operation on the stopping distance would give a result that is a linear function of the speed?
The model of the stopping distance is $s_\text{p} = v_0 t_\text{r} + \dfrac{v_0^2}{2a}$. Divide both sides by $v_0$ and compare the result with the equation of a line $y = b + kx$.

First convert the speeds to $\text{m/s}$: for example $30\,\text{km/h} = 8.33\,\text{m/s}$ and $90\,\text{km/h} = 25.0\,\text{m/s}$. Then calculate $s_\text{p} : v_0$ for each measurement and fit a line.

criteria.text: Justifies the linearisation: dividing $s_\text{p} = v_0 t_\text{r} + \dfrac{v_0^2}{2a}$ by the speed gives $\dfrac{s_\text{p}}{v_0} = t_\text{r} + \dfrac{1}{2a}\,v_0$, which is a straight line.

criteria.detail: The speeds in the unit $\text{m/s}$ by substitution, and the quantity $s_\text{p} : v_0$ in seconds for each measurement.
One straight line is fitted to the points, passing between them; $v_0\ (\text{m/s})$ on the horizontal axis, $s_\text{p} / v_0\ (\text{s})$ on the vertical axis.

parts.text: Determine the driver's reaction time and the car's deceleration from the graph.
hints: What is the quantity $s_\text{p} : v_0$ when the speed approaches zero? What does the slope of the line tell?
In the linearised model $\dfrac{s_\text{p}}{v_0} = t_\text{r} + \dfrac{1}{2a}\,v_0$, so the slope is $k = \dfrac{1}{2a}$.
Read the slope $k = \dfrac{\Delta y}{\Delta x}$ from two points of the fitted line that are far apart, not from the measured points. Then solve for $a$ in symbols.

criteria.detail: The slope from two points of the line far apart, for example $(10\,\text{m/s};\ 1.66\,\text{s})$ and $(25\,\text{m/s};\ 2.86\,\text{s})$: $k \approx 0.080\,\text{s}^2\text{/m}$; intercept about $0.86\,\text{s}$.

criteria.text: Interprets the line: the intercept is the reaction time $t_\text{r}$ and the slope is $\dfrac{1}{2a}$.

criteria.detail: $a = \dfrac{1}{2k}$
$t_\text{r} \approx 0.86\,\text{s}$ and $a \approx 6.3\,\text{m/s}^2$; results of $0.80$–$0.93\,\text{s}$ and $5.9$–$6.6\,\text{m/s}^2$ are accepted.

parts.text: What is the coefficient of friction between the tyres and the wet asphalt? Use the model to estimate the stopping distance from $100\,\text{km/h}$ on the same road, and assess how reliable the estimate is.
hints: Which force decelerates the car in locked-wheel braking on a horizontal road, and what does its magnitude depend on?
At the limit of locked-wheel braking friction gives the deceleration: $\mu mg = ma$, so $\mu = a : g$. The stopping distance is $s_\text{p} = v_0 t_\text{r} + \dfrac{v_0^2}{2a}$.

Convert $100\,\text{km/h}$ to $\text{m/s}$ and calculate the reaction distance and the braking distance separately with the values of part c). Which assumptions of the model may fail outside the measured range?

criteria.detail: On a horizontal road at the limit of locking the wheels $\mu mg = ma$, so $\mu = a : g$; $s_\text{p} = v_0 t_\text{r} + \dfrac{v_0^2}{2a}$.
$\mu \approx 6.25 : 9.81 \approx 0.64$; $100\,\text{km/h} = 27.8\,\text{m/s}$, so $s_\text{p} \approx 23.9\,\text{m} + 61.7\,\text{m} \approx 86\,\text{m}$.

The estimate is an extrapolation $10\,\text{km/h}$ beyond the measured range; it holds if the deceleration stays the same even at a high speed and the driver reacts in the same way, but aquaplaning, for example, can reduce the friction.

tasks.title: River power plant or wind farm
tasks.source_note: The municipality, the river and the numbers of the power plants are invented examples.
tasks.text:
The municipal council is considering whether to renovate an old river power plant or to build a new wind farm. Councillors have made three claims.

1. “When the wind speed increases from $6\,\text{m/s}$ to $9\,\text{m/s}$, the power of a wind turbine increases by $50\,\%$.”
2. “A hydropower plant is almost a perpetual motion machine: it produces electricity year after year without consuming anything, because the same water always flows in the river.”
3. “Raising the dam from $9\,\text{m}$ to $12\,\text{m}$ would increase the power as much as increasing the flow rate by a third.”

On average $120\,\text{m}^3\text{/s}$ flows through the river power plant, the head is now $9.0\,\text{m}$ and the efficiency $90\,\%$. The data for the wind turbines show that they do not yet run at their rated power at a wind speed of $9\,\text{m/s}$.

parts.text: Assess claim 1. Explain what the power of a wind turbine depends on and why.
hints: On which two things does the energy that the air flowing through the rotor brings each second depend? How does each depend on the wind speed?
Power is energy per unit time, $P = E : t$. In time $t$ the mass of air passing through the rotor is $m = \rho A v t$, and its kinetic energy is $\tfrac12 mv^2$.
Work out how the power depends on the speed, and calculate the ratio of the powers when the speed changes in the ratio $9 : 6$. Finally, think about when this dependence stops being valid.

criteria.text: Explains that the kinetic energy of the wind per kilogram of air is proportional to the square of the speed and the amount of air flowing through the rotor per second to the speed, so the power is proportional to the cube $v^3$.

criteria.detail: $\left(\tfrac{9}{6}\right)^3 \approx 3.4$, so the power increases by about $240\,\%$, not $50\,\%$.
The efficiency is assumed to stay the same, and above the rated power the power is limited, so the cube law does not hold.
The claim is wrong: it assumes the power is proportional to the speed.

parts.text: Assess claim 2. Explain the energy chain of a hydropower plant: where the energy of the water comes from and why not all of it is converted into electricity.
hints: Follow the energy from the water above the dam to the electricity grid: in what form is it at each stage? What lifted the water up in the first place?
Energy is neither created nor destroyed: the power plant converts it from one form to another. What does the claim “without consuming anything” say about this?
At which points in the chain does some of the energy not end up as electricity? Think about the penstock, the turbine, the generator and the motion of the water below the plant.

criteria.text: Describes the chain: the potential energy of the water is transformed into kinetic energy in the penstock, and the turbine and the generator convert it into electricity.
Explains that the potential energy of the water comes from the Sun: evaporated water rises into the air and falls as rain at a higher level, so the plant does not create energy.
Names the losses: friction in the penstock and the turbine, the heating of the generator and the kinetic energy remaining in the tailwater, so the efficiency is below $100\,\%$.

criteria.detail: The claim is wrong: the plant converts energy and is not a perpetual motion machine, even though its “fuel” is renewed.

parts.text: Assess claim 3 and calculate the present electric power of the plant.
hints: On which quantities does the power of the plant depend? What happens to the product when one factor grows by a third?
The power of the plant is $P = \eta \rho Q g h$: it is proportional to both the flow rate $Q$ and the head $h$.
Calculate the present power by substituting in SI units, and then compare how many times larger $h$ would be with the raised dam and how many times larger $Q$ would be after an increase of a third.

criteria.detail: $P = \eta \rho Q g h$: the power is proportional both to the flow rate and to the head.

criteria.text: Justifies that $12 : 9 = \tfrac43$, so raising the dam increases the power by a third, as much as a flow rate a third larger.

criteria.detail: The claim is correct, provided the efficiency stays the same and the water behind the dam does not affect the flow rate.

tasks.title: Does momentum disappear?
tasks.source_note: The report and the measurements are an invented example.
tasks.text:
A group of students studied an inelastic collision on an ordinary dynamics trolley track. Trolley A ($m_\text{A} = 0.520\,\text{kg}$) was pushed into motion, and it collided with trolley B ($m_\text{B} = 0.480\,\text{kg}$), which was at rest. The ends of the trolleys had hook-and-loop strips, so they stuck together. The group filmed the collision and used video analysis to find the velocity $v_\text{A}$ of trolley A over the last $0.20\,\text{m}$ before the collision and the common velocity $v'$ of the trolleys over the distance $0.40$–$0.80\,\text{m}$ after the point of collision.

| Test | $v_\text{A}\ (\text{m/s})$ | $v'\ (\text{m/s})$ |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | $0.452$ | $0.207$ |
| 2 | $0.622$ | $0.303$ |
| 3 | $0.781$ | $0.391$ |
| 4 | $0.901$ | $0.455$ |

The group's conclusion: “The total momentum decreased in every test. So in an inelastic collision momentum is not conserved, because part of it is turned into heat and sound.”

parts.text: By what percentage did the total momentum change in test 2?
hints: Which quantity is compared before and after the collision, and which trolleys are moving in each situation?
Before the collision only trolley A moves: $p = m_\text{A} v_\text{A}$. Afterwards the trolleys move together: $p' = (m_\text{A} + m_\text{B})\,v'$. The relative change is $\dfrac{p' - p}{p}$.
Use the values of the row of test 2. First calculate $p$ and $p'$ separately in $\text{kg} \cdot \text{m/s}$ and then convert the change to a percentage. The sign tells the direction.

criteria.detail: $p = m_\text{A} v_\text{A}$ before and $p' = (m_\text{A} + m_\text{B})\,v'$ after; relative change $\dfrac{p' - p}{p}$
$p \approx 0.323\,\text{kg} \cdot \text{m/s}$ and $p' = 0.303\,\text{kg} \cdot \text{m/s}$
Change about $-6.3\,\%$, so the momentum decreased by about $6\,\%$.

parts.text: Assess the group's conclusion. What is the difference between the measurements most likely due to?
hints: The group says that momentum turns into heat and sound. Is momentum a form of energy?
Where was the velocity $v'$ measured, and which force acts on the trolleys between the collision and the point of measurement? What does conservation of momentum require of external forces?
Calculate the relative change in momentum in each test and see how it depends on the speed. Is the difference random or systematic, and what does it tell?

criteria.text: States that kinetic energy, not momentum, is converted into internal energy and sound: momentum is not a form of energy.

criteria.detail: The common velocity was measured only $0.40$–$0.80\,\text{m}$ after the collision, when rolling resistance had already had time to slow the trolleys down; rolling resistance is an external force that changes the momentum.

The difference is systematic: the momentum decreased every time, and the relative difference is largest in the slowest test ($-12\,\%$) and smallest in the fastest ($-3\,\%$), as expected from a resistive force of constant magnitude.
The data do not show that momentum is not conserved; they agree with the conservation law when the effect of the external force is taken into account.

parts.text: Plan how to improve the experiment so that it can test conservation of momentum reliably.
hints: What happens to the trolleys between the collision and the point of measurement if the velocities are measured further away from the collision?
Which external forces act on the trolleys on the track? How can their effect be reduced or measured?

How do you conclude whether the difference between the momenta is still within the measurement accuracy? Think about repeats, the uncertainty of the speed and the mass, and measurements with different masses and speeds.

criteria.text: The velocities are measured just before and just after the collision, for example with light gates or from a video over a short distance, or the velocity is extrapolated from a $(t, v)$ graph to the moment of collision.
The effect of rolling resistance is reduced or measured: for example an air track, or the track is tilted so that a trolley moves at a constant speed.

criteria.detail: Several repeats are made, and the uncertainty of the velocity and the mass is used to estimate how large a difference in the momenta is still within the measurement precision.

criteria.text: Measurements are made with different masses and velocities and the momenta are compared; in addition the change in kinetic energy is calculated and compared with the theoretical share $\tfrac{m_\text{B}}{m_\text{A} + m_\text{B}}$.

tasks.title: A pile driver and a warming pile
tasks.source_note: The numbers of the pile driver are an invented example. The specific heat capacity of steel is a table value.
tasks.text:
On a building site steel piles are driven into the ground with a pile driver. The machine lifts a ram above the top of the pile and lets it fall freely. The ram hits the head of the pile and does not bounce, but the pile and the ram move down together until the ground stops them.

- mass of the ram $3500\,\text{kg}$, mass of the pile $1100\,\text{kg}$
- drop height $0.60\,\text{m}$
- the pile sinks $18\,\text{mm}$ deeper with one blow
- mass of the steel at the top of the pile that warms up in the blows about $30\,\text{kg}$; specific heat capacity of steel $460\,\text{J/(kg} \cdot \text{K)}$

parts.text: What is the speed of the ram just before it hits the pile?
hints: Which form of energy turns into another as the ram falls? Can air resistance be ignored for this drop?
Conservation of mechanical energy: $Mgh = \tfrac12 Mv^2$.
The mass cancels from the equation, so solve for $v$ in symbols first. The height $h$ is the drop height, not the depth the pile sinks.

criteria.detail: $Mgh = \tfrac12 Mv^2$, so $v = \sqrt{2gh}$; air resistance is small for such a short drop.
$v = \sqrt{2 \cdot 9.81\,\text{m/s}^2 \cdot 0.60\,\text{m}}$
$v \approx 3.4\,\text{m/s}$ to two significant figures like the height $0.60\,\text{m}$

parts.text: What is the common velocity of the ram and the pile just after the collision? How much kinetic energy is transformed into other forms of energy in the collision?
hints: Which quantity is conserved in a short collision in which the ram and the pile stay together?
Use the speed from part a) and the masses $3500\,\text{kg}$ and $1100\,\text{kg}$. Solve for $v'$ in symbols before substituting, and calculate the kinetic energies before and after separately.

criteria.text: Justifies conservation of momentum: the collision is so short that the impulse of the force from the ground and of the weight is small during it.

criteria.detail: $Mv = (M + m)\,v'$ and $E_\text{loss} = \tfrac12 Mv^2 - \tfrac12 (M + m)\,v'^2$
$v' \approx 2.61\,\text{m/s}$; $20\,601\,\text{J} - 15\,675\,\text{J} \approx 4.9\,\text{kJ}$
$v' \approx 2.6\,\text{m/s}$ and $E_\text{loss} \approx 4.9\,\text{kJ}$ to two significant figures

parts.text: What average force does the ground exert on the pile as the pile sinks deeper?
hints: Which forms of energy do the ram and the pile have right after the collision, and what happens to them as the pile sinks?
Work–energy principle: the kinetic energy and the decrease in potential energy are used up in the work of the force from the ground, which opposes the motion and is $-Fs$.
The sinking is $s = 18\,\text{mm} = 0.018\,\text{m}$ and the change in potential energy is $(M + m)\,g s$. Use the kinetic energy right after the collision from part b) and solve for $F$ in symbols.

criteria.detail:
The work–energy principle for the motion after the collision: $$
\begin{aligned}
&\tfrac12 (M + m)\,v'^2 + (M + m)\,g s \\
&- F s \\
&= 0
\end{aligned}
$$

criteria.text: Takes into account that the potential energy of the ram and the pile also decreases as the pile sinks.

criteria.detail: $F \approx 0.92\,\text{MN}$ to two significant figures like the distance $18\,\text{mm}$

parts.text: Assume that $40\,\%$ of the energy transformed in the collision stays in the steel at the top of the pile as internal energy. By how much does the top of the pile warm up during $50$ blows if it has no time to give off heat to the surroundings? Assess how the assumptions affect the result.
hints: How many blows are there, and what fraction of the energy of each collision stays in the steel?
The increase in internal energy is related to the warming by $\Delta U = cm\Delta T$.

The increase in internal energy is that of all $50$ blows together: $\Delta U = 50 \cdot 0.40 \cdot E_\text{loss}$, where $E_\text{loss}$ is the result of part b). Solve for $\Delta T$ in symbols. Which assumptions make the result too large or too small?

criteria.detail: $\Delta U = cm\Delta T$, where $\Delta U = 50 \cdot 0.40 \cdot E_\text{loss}$
$\Delta T \approx 7\,\text{K}$, one or two significant figures, because the share $40\,\%$ and the mass $30\,\text{kg}$ are estimates
The real warming is smaller, because the steel gives off heat to the air and to the lower parts of the pile between the blows; part of the energy goes into sound and into the ram.

tasks.title: Sled on a slope
tasks.source_note: The situation and the numbers are invented examples.
tasks.text: A student studies a sled sliding down a straight slope. The mass of the sled is $2.0\,\text{kg}$ and it starts from rest. The slope is $6.0\,\text{m}$ long, and the coefficient of sliding friction is the same all the way. Air resistance is negligible. The bottom of the slope is the zero level of potential energy. The graph shows the potential energy $E_{\text{p}0}$ of the sled at the start and its kinetic energy $E_\text{k}$ at the end.

parts.text: Determine the starting height of the sled above the bottom of the slope.
hints: What energy does the sled at rest have at the start when the zero level is at the bottom of the slope? From which point of the graph is it read?
At the start there is only potential energy: $E_{\text{p}0} = mgh$.
Read $E_{\text{p}0}$ from the top of the green bar and solve for $h$ in symbols before substituting.

criteria.detail: The initial potential energy is read from the top of the green bar: $E_{\text{p}0} = 40\,\text{J}$.
$E_{\text{p}0} = mgh$, so $h = \dfrac{E_{\text{p}0}}{mg}$.

parts.text: Calculate the work done by the friction force and the magnitude of the friction force.
hints: What do the bars of the graph tell about the energy at the start and at the end? Where has the missing part gone?
Work–energy principle: $E_{\text{p}0} + W_\text{friction} = E_\text{k}$. Friction opposes the motion, so $W_\text{friction} = -F s$.
Read $E_\text{k}$ from the top of the blue bar. The distance $s$ is the length of the slope, not the height.

criteria.detail: The final kinetic energy is read from the top of the blue bar: $E_\text{k} = 25\,\text{J}$. At the start the kinetic energy is zero, and at the end the potential energy is zero.

Energy principle: $E_{\text{p}0} + W_\text{friction} = E_\text{k}$, so $W_\text{friction} = E_\text{k} - E_{\text{p}0}$. The friction force opposes the motion: $W_\text{friction} = -F s$, so $F = \dfrac{-W_\text{friction}}{s}$.
$W_\text{friction} = 25\,\text{J} - 40\,\text{J} = -15\,\text{J}$ and $F = \dfrac{15\,\text{J}}{6.0\,\text{m}} = 2.5\,\text{N}$
$W_\text{friction} = -15\,\text{J}$ and $F = 2.5\,\text{N}$; the work is negative because the friction force is against the motion.

parts.text: Calculate the speed of the sled at the bottom of the slope. How large would the speed be without friction?
hints: What energy does the sled have at the bottom of the slope, and how is the speed obtained from it?
The kinetic energy is $E_\text{k} = \tfrac12 mv^2$. Without friction mechanical energy would be conserved: $E_{\text{p}0} = \tfrac12 mv_0^2$.

Solve for $v$ and $v_0$ in symbols. In the case with friction use the final kinetic energy of the bar, and in the frictionless case the initial potential energy. Why is the speed smaller with friction?

criteria.detail: At the bottom $E_\text{k} = \tfrac12 mv^2$, so $v = \sqrt{\dfrac{2E_\text{k}}{m}}$. Without friction the mechanical energy would be conserved: $E_{\text{p}0} = \tfrac12 mv_0^2$.
$v = \sqrt{\dfrac{2 \cdot 25\,\text{J}}{2.0\,\text{kg}}} = 5.0\,\text{m/s}$ and $v_0 = \sqrt{\dfrac{2 \cdot 40\,\text{J}}{2.0\,\text{kg}}} \approx 6.3\,\text{m/s}$

criteria.text: Concludes that friction reduces the speed by about $21\,\%$: part of the potential energy becomes internal energy, which is transferred to the surroundings as heat, so less kinetic energy remains.

parts.text: The sled is replaced by a similar sled with a mass of $3.0\,\text{kg}$. The slope and the coefficient of sliding friction stay the same. What happens to the speed at the bottom of the slope? Justify by calculation.
hints: How does the mass of the sled affect the potential energy and how does it affect the friction force?
See what happens to the mass in the equation. Check by calculation with the mass $3.0\,\text{kg}$: the new potential energy and the work of friction, and deduce the final speed.

criteria.text: Justifies that the sliding friction force $F = \mu N = \mu mg\cos\alpha$ is directly proportional to the mass, as is the potential energy $mgh$. Both the source of energy and the work of friction grow in the same ratio.

criteria.detail: $mgh - \mu mg\cos\alpha \cdot s = \tfrac12 mv^2$, in which the mass cancels: $v = \sqrt{2g\,(h - \mu\cos\alpha \cdot s)}$.

The new potential energy is $60\,\text{J}$ and the work of friction $-22.5\,\text{J}$, so $E_\text{k} = 37.5\,\text{J}$ and $v = \sqrt{\dfrac{2 \cdot 37.5\,\text{J}}{3.0\,\text{kg}}} = 5.0\,\text{m/s}$.

The speed does not change: it is still $5.0\,\text{m/s}$, because the mass does not affect the speed when air resistance is negligible. Friction does more work on the heavier sled, so more mechanical energy becomes internal energy, but the sled also has more energy to begin with.

tasks.title: A kick on a football
tasks.source_note: The situation and the numbers are invented examples.
tasks.text: A football is kicked straight upwards, and the ball is initially at rest. The mass of the ball is $0.43\,\text{kg}$. The graph shows the force with which the foot kicks the ball as a function of time. The kick is so short that gravity and air resistance can be ignored during it. The zero level is the height of the ball at the moment of the kick.

parts.text: Determine the impulse that the foot exerts on the ball.
hints: Which quantity is given by the area between the force–time graph and the time axis?
The impulse equals this area. For the area of a triangle $I = \tfrac12 F_\text{max}\,\Delta t$.
Read the height $F_\text{max}$ and the base $\Delta t$ of the triangle from the graph. Convert the time from milliseconds to seconds.

criteria.detail: The triangle in the graph has a height of $900\,\text{N}$ and a base of $12\,\text{ms}$, that is $0.012\,\text{s}$.
The impulse is the area between the force-time graph and the time axis: for a triangle $I = \tfrac12 F_\text{max}\,\Delta t$.

parts.text: With what speed does the ball leave the kick?
hints: Which quantity changes when an impulse acts on the ball? What is the momentum of the ball at the start?
Impulse–momentum principle: $I = \Delta p = mv - 0$.
Use the impulse from part a) and the mass $0.43\,\text{kg}$. Solve for $v$ in symbols first.

criteria.detail: The impulse equals the change in momentum: $I = \Delta p = mv - 0$, so $v = \dfrac{I}{m}$.
$v \approx 13\,\text{m/s}$ with two significant figures, upwards.

parts.text: Calculate the kinetic energy of the ball right after the kick and the height to which the ball would rise without air resistance.
hints: What energy does the ball have right after the kick, and why does it change during the rise?
The kinetic energy is $E_\text{k} = \tfrac12 mv^2$. Without air resistance mechanical energy is conserved: $\tfrac12 mv^2 = mgh$.
Use the speed from part b). The mass cancels from the equation for the height, so solve for $h$ in symbols. The zero level is the height of the ball at the moment of the kick.

criteria.detail: $E_\text{k} = \tfrac12 mv^2$. Without air resistance the mechanical energy is conserved: $\tfrac12 mv^2 = mgh$, so $h = \dfrac{v^2}{2g}$.
$h = \dfrac{(12.56\,\text{m/s})^2}{2 \cdot 9.81\,\text{m/s}^2} \approx 8.04\,\text{m}$
$E_\text{k} \approx 34\,\text{J}$ and $h \approx 8.0\,\text{m}$ with two significant figures.

parts.text: In a real kick the ball rises to a maximum height of $6.5\,\text{m}$. Calculate the work done by air resistance and the mean magnitude of air resistance during the rise. What happens to the energy?
hints: To what height would the ball rise without air resistance? What does the difference from the real height mean for the energy?
Work–energy principle: $E_\text{k0} + W_\text{air} = mgh_\text{measured}$. The average resistive force is $F = \dfrac{-W_\text{air}}{h_\text{measured}}$.

First calculate the potential energy of the ball at the height $6.5\,\text{m}$ and compare it with the kinetic energy of part c). What is the sign of the work, and into which form of energy has the missing energy gone?

criteria.detail: Energy principle: $E_\text{k0} + W_\text{air} = mgh_\text{measured}$, so $W_\text{air} = mgh_\text{measured} - E_\text{k0}$. Mean force: $F = \dfrac{-W_\text{air}}{h_\text{measured}}$.
$F = \dfrac{6.5\,\text{J}}{6.5\,\text{m}} \approx 1.0\,\text{N}$

criteria.text: Explains that the mechanical energy is about $19\,\%$ lower than without air resistance. It has become internal energy of the air and the ball, which is transferred to the surroundings as heat.
